_comment: Permissions granted to the pnsm-ai-svc CONTAINER (taskRoleArn).
This is the identity the application code runs as. It is the blast radius
of a remote code execution in the AI service, so it is written as a
least-privilege allow-list, not a managed policy: AmazonS3FullAccess and
AWSKeyManagementServicePowerUser would each turn one bug into the whole
account. Master plan, OWASP A01.
Attach with:
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name pnsm-ai-svc-task-role \
--policy-name pnsm-ai-svc-inline \
--policy-document file://deploy/iam/ai-svc-task-role-policy.json
Placeholders in ANGLE BRACKETS are filled by scripts/provision_aws.py.
GenerateDataKey mints a fresh DEK per enrolment; Decrypt unwraps it on
each check-in. DescribeKey lets the service confirm at boot that the
CMK exists and is enabled, so a typo'd ARN fails at deploy rather than
at the first employee's enrolment.
kms:Encrypt is NOT granted. The service never encrypts anything
directly with the CMK -- envelope encryption means the CMK only ever
wraps data keys, and GenerateDataKey already does that. Granting an
operation nothing calls is how an unused permission becomes an
attacker's primitive.
The EncryptionContext condition is the important line. Without it, a
stolen wrapped key could be redeemed for ANY employee. With it, KMS
itself refuses to unwrap unless the caller names the same purpose it
was wrapped under. app/crypto/keyproviders.py sets this context on
every call and tests/unit/test_keyproviders.py proves a mismatch is
refused.
A separate statement because S3 calls KMS on the service's behalf when
an object is written with SSE-KMS, and those calls carry S3's own
encryption context (aws:s3:arn), not ours. Folding this into the
statement above with the purpose condition would make every upload
fail with an opaque AccessDenied -- a genuinely hard failure to
diagnose, which is why it is called out here.
The via-service condition keeps the grant narrow: these two actions
are usable only through S3, never by code calling KMS directly.
Object-level only, scoped to the two prefixes the service actually
builds: refs/ and checkins/. Those two strings are REF_PREFIX and
CHECKIN_PREFIX in app/storage/keys.py, and
tests/deploy/test_manifests.py compares them -- a policy that grants a
prefix the code never writes produces an AccessDenied on every single
enrolment, in production, with nothing wrong in either file alone.
No s3:DeleteObject: retention is enforced by a bucket lifecycle rule,
so the container has no way to erase evidence of a fraudulent check-in.
PutObject is granted because the presigned PUT the mobile client uses
is signed with THIS role's credentials -- a presigned URL can never
convey a permission its signer lacks.
/ready reports the bucket's measured encryption and public-access
state rather than asserting it (app/runtime.py storage_posture). That
needs three read-only configuration calls. Bucket-level resource, no
write actions -- the service can look at the posture and cannot change
it.
An explicit Deny, which beats any Allow anywhere in the account. Cheap
insurance against a future endpoint override or an SDK misconfiguration
putting biometric data on the wire in plaintext. Master plan: TLS 1.2+
for all transit data.
